author: jurlycat
text:
Opus plans. DeepSeek implements. A test runner checks the result.

That’s the architecture behind Cheap Agent, an open-source tool for Claude Code.

Opus writes a task specification. A cheaper worker reads the code, writes a failing test, and implements the fix inside an isolated git worktree.

The harness runs the tests itself. Passing changes land uncommitted for human review. If the worker gets stuck, a Sonnet helper can take over.

In the author’s feature demo:
154k → 57k Opus tokens. A 63% reduction.

On small SWE-bench Verified subsets:

→ Everyday bugs: 59% fewer Opus tokens, both setups solved 7/7.
→ Hard bugs: 55% fewer Opus tokens, Cheap Agent solved 6/9 versus 7/9 for plain Opus.

These are author-reported results from small samples. Savings measure Opus tokens; total cost also includes workers and helpers.

What makes this interesting is the context budget.

Every source file, test log, and retry handled by a worker reduces what the expensive model needs to process.

Give the planner concise results, give workers clear boundaries, and build an escalation path for failures.

The orchestration architecture can matter as much as the model you choose.
